dynasties.description: A South Indian dynasty that ruled from Kanchipuram and was among the first to raise structural stone temples in the Tamil country. The Pallavas patronised Sanskrit and Tamil learning and their inscriptions (in Sanskrit/Grantha and Tamil) are foundational sources for early Tamil epigraphy.
dynasties.sourceNote: Chronology per standard reference works (e.g. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India). The Pallava period is conventionally c. 3rd–9th century CE.

dynasties.description: The medieval Chola empire was the great age of Tamil temple-building and of epigraphic production. Chola inscriptions — in Tamil and Sanskrit (Grantha) — record grants, temple administration, army and village organisation, and the construction of the great Rajarajesvaram and Rajendracolapuram temples.
dynasties.sourceNote: Conventional dates for the medieval (Later) Chola line, c. 848–1279 CE (e.g. Nilakanta Sastri).

dynasties.description: A Tamil dynasty centred on Madurai, contemporary with the Cholas and Pandyas, whose later inscriptions appear at several Chola-period temples after their resurgence in the 13th century.
dynasties.sourceNote: Later Pandya resurgence conventionally dated c. 1190–1310 CE.

dynasties.description: The Vijayanagara empire of Karnataka patronised temples across the Tamil country in its later phase; a Vijayanagara-period record (Saka 1408 = 1486 CE) is found at Darasuram.
The Nayak rulers (Madurai, Thanjavur, Gingee) were Vijayanagara successors who endowed and expanded many Tamil temples in the 16th–17th centuries.
dynasties.sourceNote: Tamil Nayak polities conventionally dated 16th–18th centuries CE.

rulers.note: Pallava king credited with early rock-cut (mandapa) temples; an early Tamil inscription in Grantha script at Mamallapuram is attributed to him.

Pallava king who built the Kailasanathar Temple at Kanchipuram and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram. His Sanskrit foundation inscriptions in Grantha script record the titles Rajasimha and Atyantakama.
The great Chola emperor who built the Rajarajesvaram (Brihadisvara) temple at Thanjavur and caused its walls to be covered with inscriptions recording endowments, temple servants, and his conquests.
Son and successor of Rajaraja I; assumed the title Gangaikonda ('the Chola who took the Ganga') after a northern campaign, and built the Rajendracolapuram temple at Gangaikondacholapuram.
Chola king who sacked Kalyani; a war-trophy dvarapala inscription from that campaign was later housed at Darasuram.

Chola king whose historical introduction (meykirtti) is inscribed at Darasuram. A Chidambaram inscription (SII XII, No. 149) is dated in the 6th year of the feudatory 'Sakalabhuvanachakravartti Avaniyalappirandar alias Kopperunjingadeva'.
Chola king who built the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram. Darasuram inscriptions are dated in his regnal years (e.g. 21st year ≈ 1167 CE).
Chola king named in Darasuram inscriptions (e.g. ARE 18, 19 of 1908).
Chola king named in a Darasuram inscription (ARE 20 of 1908, 8th year ≈ 1186 CE) recording a gift for gilding the sikhara of the temple.
Pandya king named in a Darasuram inscription (ARE 21 of 1908, 3rd year).
Pandya king named in a Darasuram inscription (ARE 23 of 1908) providing for repairs and festivals.

districts.note: District headquarters at Thanjavur; home to the Brihadisvara (Rajarajesvaram) temple.
Gangaikondacholapuram is in Ariyalur district (reorganised from Perambalur/Thanjavur).
Darasuram (Airavatesvara temple) lies within the Kumbakonam taluk of Thanjavur district.
Kanchipuram district; seat of the Pallava Kailasanathar temple.
Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) is in Chengalpattu district (reorganised from Kanchipuram).
Chidambaram is in Cuddalore district (reorganised from South Arcot).

temples.alternateNames: Peruvudaiyar Kovil, Periya Kovil, Tanjore Big Temple, Rajarajesvara Temple
temples.periodNote: Built and consecrated in the reign of Rajaraja I; the temple walls carry dozens of contemporary Chola inscriptions of Rajaraja I, Rajendra I and others.
temples.managedBy: Archaeological Survey of India (monument); worship administered by the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department, Tamil Nadu
temples.history: The Brihadisvara Temple, called Rajarajesvaram in its own inscriptions, was built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I and consecrated around 1010 CE. It is the largest and one of the most complete surviving Chola temples, and its walls preserve a remarkable corpus of contemporary inscriptions that record the king's conquests, the temple's endowments, the organisation of its staff, and the measurement and valuation of its gifts. With the temples at Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram it forms the UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples' property.
temples.architecture: Built of granite, the temple is famed for its towering vimana (the srivimana) rising in thirteen diminishing tiers to about 66 m, capped by a single 80-tonne granite block (the sikhara / kumbham). The complex includes a massive Nandi hall, a colonnaded precinct (the south, west and north enclosures carry inscriptions on their pillars and walls), and an exceptional programme of Chola sculpture and bronze icons. The inscriptions of Rajaraja I are engraved on the basal and upper tiers of the central shrine and on the enclosure walls.
temples.summary: The great Rajaraja I temple at Thanjavur — a UNESCO World Heritage monument and the richest single source of Chola epigraphy, with its walls recording the temple's endowments, administration and the king's conquests.
temples.sourceNote: Coordinates 10.7828°N, 79.1318°E (multiple gazetteers). UNESCO World Heritage ref. 250 (inscribed 1987, extended 2004). Inscriptions: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II (Rajarajesvaram temple), ed. V. Venkayya, ASI NIS Vol. X, 1913.

temples.periodNote: Built by Rajendra I after his northern campaign; the city was the Chola capital in the 11th century.
temples.history: Gangaikondacholapuram ('the town of the Chola who took the Ganga') was founded by Rajendra I to commemorate his victorious northern campaign. He built there the Rajendracolapuram temple, a planned parallel to his father's Rajarajesvaram at Thanjavur, and made the city the Chola capital. The temple's inscriptions record the king's titles and endowments.
temples.architecture: The temple repeats the axial plan of the Thanjavur Brihadisvara but is more elongated; its vimana is slightly shorter yet remarkable for its graceful batter. The precinct contains fine Chola bronze icons and sculpture, and the great water-tank (Cholagangam) lies nearby. The inscriptions of Rajendra I are found on the temple walls and basement.
temples.summary: Rajendra I's capital-city temple — a UNESCO Great Living Chola Temple and the ceremonial heart of the 11th-century Chola empire.
temples.sourceNote: Coordinates ≈ 11.2048°N, 79.4517°E (Gangaikondacholapuram village, Ariyalur district). UNESCO ref. 250. Foundation/endowment inscriptions of Rajendra I are published in South Indian Inscriptions and the Annual Reports on (South) Indian Epigraphy.

temples.alternateNames: Darasuram Temple, Rajarajesvaram Udaiya Nayanar at Rajarajapuram
temples.periodNote: Built by Rajaraja Chola II (c. 1146–1173); inscriptions dated in his regnal years (e.g. 21st year ≈ 1167 CE).
temples.history: The Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram was built by Rajaraja Chola II and named Rajarajesvaram Udaiya Nayanar at Rajarajapuram. Its inscriptions (ARE 16–27 of 1908) record the temple's history, endowments and repairs across the Chola, Pandya and Vijayanagara periods. A war-trophy dvarapala inscription of Rajadhiraja I, taken after the sack of Kalyani (c. 1054 CE), was later housed here.
temples.architecture: The temple is celebrated for its articulated mandapa (often compared to a stone chariot, with 'musical' steps) and its rich sculptural friezes. Inscriptions are engraved on the central shrine basement, the east and south walls, the inner gopuram, and stones in the courtyard. The Amman shrine (Deiva Nayaki) is associated with a Kulottunga III inscription (ARE 20 of 1908).
temples.summary: Rajaraja Chola II's jewel-like Chola temple at Darasuram — a UNESCO Great Living Chola Temple and a treasury of later-Chola inscriptions.
temples.sourceNote: Coordinates ≈ 10.9547°N, 79.4356°E (Darasuram, Thanjavur district). UNESCO ref. 250. Inscriptions: Annual Report on Indian Epigraphy 1908, Nos. 16–27 (Darasuram); see K. V. Subrahmanya Aiyer, Later Chola Temples.

temples.periodNote: Built by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), c. 700–728 CE; completed/expanded by his son Mahendravarman II.
temples.history: The Kailasanathar Temple is the earliest major structural stone temple at Kanchipuram and a landmark of Pallava architecture. Sanskrit foundation inscriptions in the Grantha script record the builder's titles (Rajasimha, Atyantakama). It marks the transition from rock-cut to structural temple-building in the Tamil country.
temples.architecture: Built of sandstone, the temple has a pyramidal vimana surrounded by a courtyard wall lined with 58 (traditionally counted) small shrines (parivara devatas). The plinths and inner enclosure carry Pallava Sanskrit inscriptions; the sculptural programme includes exquisite panels of Shiva and the river goddesses.
temples.summary: The Pallava sandstone masterpiece at Kanchipuram — among the earliest structural temples in the Tamil country, with Sanskrit/Grantha foundation inscriptions of Rajasimha.
temples.sourceNote: Coordinates ≈ 12.8436°N, 79.6993°E. Inscriptions: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I (Pallava inscriptions of Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram), ed. E. Hultzsch, ASI NIS Vol. I. Builder: Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), c. 700–728 CE.

temples.alternateNames: Mahabalipuram Shore Temple, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram
temples.periodNote: Structural temple built of granite under Narasimhavarman II, c. 700–728 CE; the surrounding monuments span the Pallava period.
temples.history: The Shore Temple is the surviving structural temple at the head of the Group of Monuments at Mamallapuram, built by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha). It stands on a granite promontory above the Bay of Bengal and was historically part of the 'Seven Pagodas' complex. The site is inscribed by UNESCO as the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram.
temples.architecture: Built of dressed granite blocks, the temple comprises shrines to Shiva (east and west) and a Vishnu shrine, fronted by a miniature vimana and rock-cut lions. Subsequent coastal erosion has been mitigated by a protective breakwater. Pallava inscriptions at the site include the Sanskrit/Grantha records of Rajasimha and the Tamil records of his predecessor Mahendravarman I.
temples.summary: The Pallava structural temple on the shore at Mamallapuram — the surviving centrepiece of a UNESCO World Heritage group of monuments.
temples.sourceNote: Coordinates ≈ 12.6164°N, 80.1917°E. UNESCO ref. 249 (inscribed 1984). Builder: Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), c. 700–728 CE. Inscriptions: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I.

temples.deity: Shiva as Nataraja (the dancing Shiva); Akasa Lingam
temples.patron: Chola royalty (notably Rajaraja I and later Cholas); earlier Pallava roots
temples.periodNote: An ancient Shiva centre; major Chola endowments from the 10th–13th centuries, with later Nayak and Vijayanagara additions. Inscriptions span the Chola, Pandya and Vijayanagara periods.
temples.managedBy: The temple is administered by a hereditary dikshitar (sthapatis) management and the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department, Tamil Nadu
temples.history: Chidambaram is one of the holiest Shiva centres (the Todai mangalam / Tillai) and the home of the Nataraja icon. It was a favoured royal temple of the Cholas; Rajaraja I and later Chola kings are associated with its patronage, and its walls carry many inscriptions (e.g. SII XII, Nos. 149, 151) recording temple administration, committees and flower-garden endowments. The sanctum (Chit Sabha) houses the Akasa Lingam (the 'empty' linga symbolising space).
temples.architecture: The complex is enclosed by four towering gopurams and contains the golden-roofed Chit Sabha (Kanaka Sabha) before the Nataraja sanctum. The 108 karanas (poses) of Bharatanatyam are sculpted on the northern gopuram. Inscriptions line the walls of the prakaras (e.g. the north wall of the third prakara).
temples.summary: The great Chola royal temple of Nataraja at Chidambaram — a living centre of Tamil devotional and dance tradition, rich in Chola inscriptions on temple administration.
temples.sourceNote: Coordinates ≈ 11.3993°N, 79.6935°E. Inscriptions: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. XII (Chidambaram), ed. S. R. Balasubrahmanyam / T. V. Mahalingam (ASI NIS). SII XII, Nos. 149, 151 = A.R. Nos. 296 & 304 of 1913 (Chidambaram, South Arcot).

inscriptions.title: List of silver utensils presented by Rajaraja I
inscriptions.areNumber: Not re-numbered in ARE (published in SII Vol. II)
inscriptions.siiReference: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, No. 91
inscriptions.dateNote: Dated in the reign of Rajaraja I; the inscription is on the lower tier of the north wall of the central shrine.
inscriptions.physicalLocation: North wall of the central shrine (srivimana), lower tier, Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur.
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Original Tamil text published in SII Vol. II; not transcribed here to avoid OCR errors. See source citation.
inscriptions.translation: This inscription contains a list of silver utensils presented by king Rajaraja-deva to the temple. They are said to have borne the names Sivapida-Sekaran and Sri-Rajarajan and to have been procured from three sources: (1) the king's treasures, (2) the booty acquired in the war against the Chera king and the Pandyas in Malai-nadu, and (3) the silver seized in the same campaign. The list begins with the gifts made from the treasures seized after defeating the Chera king and the Pandyas in Malai-nadu. At the end of the inscription three silver images of Sri-Vasudeva are mentioned. This is the only inscription of the temple which mentions presents made of silver; most others record gifts of gold.
inscriptions.translationSource: English translation/summary by V. Venkayya, SII Vol. II, pp. 416–418 (Rajarajesvaram temple inscriptions).
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: King Rajaraja I gave the temple a large set of silver vessels and three silver images of Vishnu. Some of the silver came from his own treasury and some from plunder taken when he defeated the Chera and Pandya kings in the Malai-nadu (Kerala) campaign. Unusually for this temple, this record lists silver rather than gold gifts.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: Documents Rajaraja I's Kerala campaign (war against the Chera and Pandya kings in Malai-nadu) and the royal practice of endowing the Rajarajesvaram temple with vessels and images. It is the only Thanjavur inscription among Venkayya's volume that records silver (not gold) gifts, valuable for understanding the temple's material economy.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Venkayya, V. (ed. & trans.), South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II — Tamil Inscriptions of Rajaraja, Rajendra-Chola and others in the Rajarajesvara Temple at Tanjavur, Part IV, No. 91, pp. 416–418. Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series, Vol. X, Madras, 1913.

inscriptions.title: Jewelled ornaments presented by the king from Chera–Pandya spoils
inscriptions.siiReference: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, No. 93
inscriptions.dateNote: Dated in the reign of Rajaraja I; on the south wall, third tier of the central shrine.
inscriptions.physicalLocation: South wall of the central shrine (srivimana), third tier, Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur.
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Original Tamil text published in SII Vol. II; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: This inscription enumerates the jewelled ornaments presented by the king out of the treasures seized from the Cheras and Pandyas and out of his own treasures. They comprise necklaces, armlets, bracelets, rings, and sandals made of wood covered with gold plates and set with jewels. Four of the rings had the nine gems set on them — diamond, sapphire, pearl, topaz, cinnamon stone, coral, emerald, lapis lazuli and ruby. The mention of the nine gems occurs only here among the Tanjore inscriptions.
inscriptions.translationSource: English translation/summary by V. Venkayya, SII Vol. II, pp. 429–431 (Rajarajesvaram temple inscriptions).
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: Rajaraja I gave the temple a catalogue of jewelled ornaments — necklaces, armlets, rings and bejewelled sandals — made from the spoils taken from the defeated Chera and Pandya kings as well as from his own treasury. Four rings were set with the traditional nine gems. This is the only Thanjavur inscription that lists the nine gems.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: Records the conversion of war-spoils (from the Chola victories over the Chera and Pandya kings) into temple wealth, and preserves a rare explicit list of the 'nine gems' (navaratna) in a Chola inscription.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Venkayya, V. (ed. & trans.), South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, No. 93, pp. 429–431. Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series, Vol. X, Madras, 1913.

inscriptions.title: Inscription on the outside of the north enclosure
inscriptions.siiReference: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, No. 94
inscriptions.dateNote: On the outside of the north enclosure of the Rajarajesvaram temple.
inscriptions.physicalLocation: Outside of the north enclosure (northern precinct wall), Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur.
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Original Tamil text published in SII Vol. II; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: This inscription is engraved on the outer face of the northern enclosure wall of the Rajarajesvaram temple. (The published text records the standard royal introduction of Rajaraja I and the details of endowments; the precise content of the damaged portions is summarised by the editor rather than freely translated here.)
inscriptions.translationSource: SII Vol. II, No. 94, pp. 439–449; summary after V. Venkayya.
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: One of the Rajaraja I records on the outer north enclosure wall of the temple, recording royal endowments. The editor notes that parts are damaged.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: Part of the continuous band of Rajaraja I inscriptions around the temple's enclosures, essential for reconstructing the temple's endowment history.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Venkayya, V. (ed. & trans.), South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, No. 94, pp. 439–449. Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series, Vol. X, Madras, 1913.

inscriptions.title: Committee and flower-garden endowment at Chidambaram
inscriptions.titleTa: சிதம்பரம் கோயில் குழு மற்றும் மலர் தோட்ட நன்கொடை
inscriptions.referenceId: SII Vol. XII, No. 149 (A.R. No. 296 of 1913)
inscriptions.siiReference: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. XII, No. 149
inscriptions.regnalYear: 6th year of Sakalabhuvanachakravartti Avaniyalappirandar alias Kopperunjingadeva
inscriptions.dateNote: Dated in the 6th year of the feudatory chief Kopperunjingadeva (a subordinate of the Chola emperor Kulottunga I).
inscriptions.physicalLocation: North wall of the third prakara, Nataraja Temple, Chidambaram.
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Original Tamil text published in SII Vol. XII; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: This inscription gives an insight into the management of the temple affairs. It is dated in the 6th year of Sakalabhuvanachakravartti Avaniyalappirandar alias Kopperunjingadeva. The temple at Chidambaram was at this time managed by a committee consisting of the following members and groups: Jayatungap-Pallavaraiyar, Tillaiambalap-Pallavaraiyar, Mahesvara-kankaniseyvar, Srikaryamseyvar, Samudayancheyvar, Koyilanayakancheyar, Tirumaligaikkuruseyvar and the accountants. It registers a grant of land made by Sottai-Nayaka alias Kumara-Bhatta of Irayur, residing in Ponmeyndasola-chaturvedimangalam, for a flower garden called 'Tirunilai-Alagiya' for supplying flowers to the god and the goddess Tirukkamakkottamudaiya Periyanachchiyar, with an additional plot purchased from Ponnandi for the maintenance of the gardener.
inscriptions.translationSource: English summary by the editor, SII Vol. XII, No. 149 (A.R. No. 296 of 1913).
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: A record of how the Chidambaram temple was run by a committee of officers and groups, and of a land-gift to maintain a flower garden that supplied garlands to the god and goddess. It shows the organised, committee-based administration of a great temple.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: A rare, detailed view of medieval South Indian temple administration — the named committee, the flower-garden endowment, and the use of a brahmadeya village (Ponmeyndasola-chaturvedimangalam, named after Kulottunga Chola II) for temple service.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. XII (Chidambaram), No. 149 = A.R. No. 296 of 1913, on the north wall of the third prakara, Nataraja Temple, Chidambaram (then South Arcot district). Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series.

inscriptions.title: Order of the officer Solakon to engrave a flower-garden gift
inscriptions.titleTa: சோழகோன் அதிகாரியின் ஆணை: மலர் தோட்ட நன்கொடை
inscriptions.referenceId: SII Vol. XII, No. 151 (A.R. No. 304 of 1913)
inscriptions.siiReference: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. XII, No. 151
inscriptions.dateNote: Dated in the 7th year; order issued by the officer Solakon to the temple authorities.
inscriptions.physicalLocation: North wall of the third prakara, Nataraja Temple, Chidambaram.
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Original Tamil text published in SII Vol. XII; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: This inscription, dated in the 7th year, contains an order of the officer Solakon issued to the authorities of the temple at Chidambaram, to engrave on their temple walls the gift of a flower garden made after purchase by a devaradiyar named Pillaiyar Sirridai Arivai and one Irangalmitta-pillaiyar.
inscriptions.translationSource: English summary by the editor, SII Vol. XII, No. 151 (A.R. No. 304 of 1913).
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: A temple officer (Solakon) instructed the Chidambaram authorities to record on the temple wall a flower-garden gift bought by two women devotees (devaradiyars). It shows how private devotional gifts were officially registered on temple walls.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: Illustrates the role of women devotees (devaradiyars) as donors and the bureaucratic process by which gifts were authenticated and engraved at a major temple.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. XII (Chidambaram), No. 151 = A.R. No. 304 of 1913, on the north wall of the third prakara, Nataraja Temple, Chidambaram (then South Arcot district). Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series.

inscriptions.title: Darasuram inscription of Rajaraja Chola II (21st year)
inscriptions.regnalYear: 21st year of Tribhuvana Chakravartin Rajaraja (II) (≈ A.D. 1167)
inscriptions.dateNote: Dated in the 21st regnal year of Rajaraja Chola II (c. 1146–1173), i.e. about 1167 CE.
inscriptions.physicalLocation: East Wall, first prakara, Airavatesvara Temple, Darasuram.
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Text published in the Annual Report on Indian Epigraphy 1908; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: Inscription of the 21st year of Tribhuvana Chakravartin Rajaraja (II), recording a royal order/donation connected with the Airavatesvara (Rajarajesvaram Udaiya Nayanar) temple at Rajarajapuram (Darasuram). (The editor's summary is used here to avoid presenting an unverified free translation.)
inscriptions.translationSource: Annual Report on Indian Epigraphy 1908, No. 17 (Darasuram); summarised in K. V. Subrahmanya Aiyer, Later Chola Temples.
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: A record from the 21st year of Rajaraja Chola II at the very temple he built, documenting a royal donation or order for the Airavatesvara temple.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: Directly ties the builder-king Rajaraja II to his foundation at Darasuram and helps fix the temple's construction date within his reign.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Annual Report on Indian Epigraphy 1908, No. 17 (Darasuram, East Wall, 1st prakara). Government of India / Archaeological Survey of India. Also K. V. Subrahmanya Aiyer, Later Chola Temples.

inscriptions.title: Gift for gilding the sikhara (Kulottunga III, 8th year)
inscriptions.titleTa: விமானக் கலசம் பொன்னிற்கான நன்கொடை (மூன்றாம் குலோத்துங்கன், 8ஆம் ஆண்டு)
inscriptions.regnalYear: 8th year of Parakesari Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulottunga (III) (≈ A.D. 1186)
inscriptions.dateNote: Dated in the 8th regnal year of Kulottunga Chola III, about 1186 CE.
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Text published in the Annual Report on Indian Epigraphy 1908; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: South Wall inscription of the 8th year of Kulottunga Chola III recording a gift of land for repairs and for gilding the sikhara (finial/vimana crown) of the temple of Rajarajesvaram Udaiya Nayanar at Rajarajapuram. The editor notes that the Amman Temple for Deiva Nayaki was likely built at this time.
inscriptions.translationSource: Annual Report on Indian Epigraphy 1908, No. 20 (Darasuram); summarised in K. V. Subrahmanya Aiyer, Later Chola Temples.
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: A later Chola king, Kulottunga III, gave land to repair the temple and to gild its tower; this record also hints that the goddess (Amman) shrine was built then.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: Shows the continuing royal patronage and maintenance of the Darasuram temple generations after its foundation, and helps date the Deiva Nayaki (Amman) shrine.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Annual Report on Indian Epigraphy 1908, No. 20 (Darasuram, South Wall). Government of India / Archaeological Survey of India. Also K. V. Subrahmanya Aiyer, Later Chola Temples.

inscriptions.title: War-trophy dvarapala of Vijaya-Rajendra (sack of Kalyani)
inscriptions.regnalYear: About A.D. 1054 (Vijaya-Rajendra / Rajadhiraja I after the sack of Kalyani)
inscriptions.dateNote: Records the celebration of a virabhishekam after the Chola sack of Kalyani (c. 1054 CE) by Rajadhiraja I (Vijaya-Rajendra).
inscriptions.physicalLocation: At the base of a dvarapala image (brought by Vijaya-Rajendra after the sack of Kalyani); found on the front platform on the outer (eastern) side of the inner gopuram, now housed in the Thanjavur Art Gallery.
inscriptions.originalText: Svasti Sri Udaiyar Sri Vijaya Rajendra devar Kalyanapuram erindu kodu vanda dvarapalar
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Transcribed in ARE 1908, No. 24; also quoted in K. V. Subrahmanya Aiyer, Later Chola Temples.
inscriptions.translation: 'Hail! The auspicious Lord Sri Vijaya-Rajendra-deva, having taken (eridu) Kalyanapuram (Kalyani), brought (this) dvarapala.' The inscription celebrates Rajadhiraja I (Vijaya-Rajendra) bringing a temple-guardian (dvarapala) image as war-spoil after the Chola victory at Kalyani.
inscriptions.translationSource: Translation/gloss of the Tamil text in ARE 1908, No. 24 and Later Chola Temples.
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: A short label on a stone temple-guardian statue taken from Kalyani as war-booty by the Chola king Rajadhiraja I, later kept at Darasuram and now in the Thanjavur Art Gallery.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: A tangible war-trophy inscription linking the later-Chola temple at Darasuram to the Chola victory over the Western Chalukyas at Kalyani (c. 1054 CE); a caution against attributing the Darasuram temple itself to that campaign, since Rajaraja II built it a century later.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Annual Report on Indian Epigraphy 1908, No. 24 (Darasuram). Also K. V. Subrahmanya Aiyer, Later Chola Temples (Appendix 2).

inscriptions.title: Endowment inscription of Rajendra I (Gangaikondacholapuram)
inscriptions.areNumber: Published in ARE (Gangaikondacholapuram); see source note
inscriptions.siiReference: South Indian Inscriptions (Chola inscriptions); Gangaikondacholapuram volume
inscriptions.dateNote: Dated in the reign of Rajendra I, founder of Gangaikondacholapuram.
inscriptions.physicalLocation: Basement and walls of the Rajendracolapuram temple, Gangaikondacholapuram. (Precise location not independently re-verified here; recorded in the published Annual Reports.)
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Original Tamil text in the published Gangaikondacholapuram inscriptions; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: The Gangaikondacholapuram inscriptions of Rajendra I record the king's assumption of the title Gangaikonda ('he who took the Ganga') after his northern campaign, and the endowments he made to the Rajendracolapuram temple, its staff and services.
inscriptions.translationSource: Summary from the published Gangaikondacholapuram inscriptions (SII / ARE) and standard histories (e.g. Nilakanta Sastri).
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: Rajendra I recorded at his new capital-temple the title he won by his northern conquest and the gifts he made to maintain the temple.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: The foundational inscriptions of the Chola imperial capital and its great temple; they anchor the dating of Rajendra I's reign and the Gangaikondacholapuram foundation.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Annual Report(s) on Indian Epigraphy — Gangaikondacholapuram; South Indian Inscriptions (Chola inscriptions). See also K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas.

inscriptions.title: Sanskrit foundation inscription of Rajasimha (Kailasanatha)
inscriptions.siiReference: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I (Pallava inscriptions of Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram)
inscriptions.regnalYear: Reign of Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), c. 700–728 CE
inscriptions.dateNote: Dated in the reign of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, who took the title Rajasimha.
inscriptions.physicalLocation: On the plinths and inner enclosure walls of the Kailasanathar Temple, Kanchipuram. (Precise inscription number not independently re-verified here; recorded in SII Vol. I.)
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Original Sanskrit/Grantha text in SII Vol. I; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: The Pallava Sanskrit foundation inscriptions of the Kailasanathar Temple record the builder's royal titles — Rajasimha and Atyantakama — and praise the construction of the Shiva temple at Kanchipuram. (The full edited text/translation is in SII Vol. I; a free translation is not reproduced here to avoid error.)
inscriptions.translationSource: E. Hultzsch (ed.), South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I — Pallava inscriptions of Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram, ASI NIS Vol. I.
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: The builder-king Rajasimha left Sanskrit inscriptions in Grantha script on the temple, recording his titles and the founding of the Kailasanathar Temple.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: Among the earliest structural-temple foundation inscriptions in the Tamil country; they identify the patron (Rajasimha/Narasimhavarman II) and mark the Pallava shift from rock-cut to structural architecture.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Hultzsch, E. (ed.), South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I, Pallava Inscriptions (Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram). Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series, Vol. I.

inscriptions.title: Pallava inscriptions of the Group of Monuments at Mamallapuram
inscriptions.siiReference: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I (Pallava inscriptions of Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram)
inscriptions.regnalYear: Reign of Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), c. 700–728 CE (with earlier records of Mahendravarman I)
inscriptions.dateNote: Includes the Sanskrit/Grantha records of Rajasimha and the early Tamil record of Mahendravarman I at Mamallapuram.
inscriptions.physicalLocation: Across the Group of Monuments at Mamallapuram ( Shore Temple, rock-cut caves, rathas and the bas-relief panels). (Precise numbers not independently re-verified here; recorded in SII Vol. I.)
inscriptions.originalTextSource: Original texts in SII Vol. I; see source citation.
inscriptions.translation: The Mamallapuram inscriptions include the Sanskrit/Grantha records of the builder-king Rajasimha and an early Tamil inscription in Grantha script attributed to Mahendravarman I. They name the patron kings and record the religious foundations of the Pallava port-city.
inscriptions.translationSource: E. Hultzsch (ed.), South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I, Pallava Inscriptions (Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram).
inscriptions.simpleExplanation: The monuments at Mamallapuram carry Pallava inscriptions — in Sanskrit/Grantha and Tamil — that name the kings who built them, especially Rajasimha and his father Mahendravarman I.
inscriptions.historicalSignificance: Core epigraphic evidence for the dating and patronage of the UNESCO Group of Monuments at Mamallapuram, one of the most important Pallava sites.
inscriptions.sourceCitation: Hultzsch, E. (ed.), South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I, Pallava Inscriptions (Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram). Archaeological Survey of India, New Imperial Series, Vol. I.
